# Cleaning Script {.unnumbered} ::: {.lead} Data Cleaning Rebuild — Raw to Final Master Dataset :::

## Load the raw data This script cleans and matches the raw homicide, law enforcement agency, and weather datasets, then saves the final dataset as two Parquet file. Each step stays in the order it was done, including checks that led to later fixes. But first, I'll load in the required packages. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Load libraries. #== packages == library(here) library(readr) library(dplyr) library(tidyr) library(ggplot2) library(lubridate) library(rmarkdown) library(sessioninfo) ``` :::
::: {.content-hidden when-profile="book"} The function, `load_raw_data()`, uses `here::here()` to build each file's path from the project folder, `read_csv()` to read it, and `stopifnot()` to stop the run if the row count doesn't match the expected number: 894,636 homicide records, 23,486 agency records, and 89,121 weather records. And it lives in the utils.R file, along with all the other functions, and will be called in with the `source()`. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Source the load_raw_data function. # (Buck, 2025; Olumide, 2025) source( here::here( "scripts", "utils.R" ) ) ``` ::: My custom `load_raw_data()` function is run, and `$` pulls each of the three datasets out of the list it returns, so each one can be worked with on its own. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Load the data into a list. #== assign the load function == # (Buck, 2025) raw_data <- load_raw_data() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` Rows: 894636 Columns: 30 ── Column specification ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────── Delimiter: "," chr (23): ID, CNTYFIPS, Ori, State, Agency, Agentype, Source, Solved, Month,... dbl (7): Year, Incident, VicAge, OffAge, VicCount, OffCount, FileDate ℹ Use `spec()` to retrieve the full column specification for this data. ℹ Specify the column types or set `show_col_types = FALSE` to quiet this message. Rows: 89121 Columns: 19 ── Column specification ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────── Delimiter: "," chr (8): timezone, timezone_abbreviation, daily_units.time, daily_units.te... dbl (10): latitude, longitude, generationtime_ms, utc_offset_seconds, eleva... date (1): daily.time ℹ Use `spec()` to retrieve the full column specification for this data. ℹ Specify the column types or set `show_col_types = FALSE` to quiet this message. ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` All raw row counts confirmed. ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} #== access individual dataframes == homicide_df <- raw_data$homicide geojson_df <- raw_data$geojson weather_df <- raw_data$weather ``` ::: Then, after loading the data into the list, *"All raw row counts confirmed"* message outputs, which confirms that the row count check passed for all three files. This second custom function, `column_list()`, uses the `names()` to list each dataset's column names so the raw columns can be compared before any are renamed. The `source()` will dynamically call in this custom function, too. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Inspect the column names of each raw dataset. #== call the column list function == # (Buck, 2025) display_columns <- column_list( data1 = homicide_df, data2 = geojson_df, data3 = weather_df ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` All datasets returned. ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} display_columns ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` $homicide_list [1] "ID" "CNTYFIPS" "Ori" "State" "Agency" [6] "Agentype" "Source" "Solved" "Year" "Month" [11] "Incident" "ActionType" "Homicide" "Situation" "VicAge" [16] "VicSex" "VicRace" "VicEthnic" "OffAge" "OffSex" [21] "OffRace" "OffEthnic" "Weapon" "Relationship" "Circumstance" [26] "Subcircum" "VicCount" "OffCount" "FileDate" "MSA" $geojson_list [1] "OBJECTID" "ID" "NAME" "ADDRESS" "CITY" [6] "STATE" "ZIP" "ZIP4" "TELEPHONE" "TYPE" [11] "STATUS" "POPULATION" "COUNTY" "COUNTYFIPS" "COUNTRY" [16] "LATITUDE" "LONGITUDE" "NAICS_CODE" "NAICS_DESC" "SOURCE" [21] "SOURCEDATE" "VAL_METHOD" "VAL_DATE" "WEBSITE" "CI_ID" [26] "CSLLEA08ID" "SUBTYPE1" "SUBTYPE2" "TRIBAL" "NUMPRE" [31] "NUMFIXSUB" "NUMMOBILE" "FTSWORN" "FTCIV" "PTSWORN" [36] "PTCIV" "geometry" $weather_list [1] "latitude" [2] "longitude" [3] "generationtime_ms" [4] "utc_offset_seconds" [5] "timezone" [6] "timezone_abbreviation" [7] "elevation" [8] "daily_units.time" [9] "daily_units.temperature_2m_mean" [10] "daily_units.rain_sum" [11] "daily_units.snowfall_sum" [12] "daily_units.relative_humidity_2m_mean" [13] "daily.time" [14] "daily.temperature_2m_mean" [15] "daily.rain_sum" [16] "daily.snowfall_sum" [17] "daily.relative_humidity_2m_mean" [18] "location_id" [19] "state_territory" ``` ::: ::: Each dataframe (DF) writes its column names its own way. The **homicide DF** uses a mix of all-capital names and capitalized short words, some run together (e.g., *CNTYFIPS* and *VicAge*). The **agency DF** uses mostly all-capital letters, for example, *POPULATION*, and the **weather DF** uses lowercase words, many starting with a prefix and a period, such as *daily.rain_sum*. Because the three styles don't match, the next stage renames the columns it works with so they follow one shared style.
## Rename the columns and check the victim categories Before renaming anything, I'll set up my third custom function, `check_column_counts()`, which uses `ncol()` to count each DF's columns. It's written in the **utils.R** file but will run after the renaming, so its defaults already point to the renamed DFs. Then, `rename()` gives the columns I work with new lowercase names joined by underscores, such as *victim_age* and *agency_population*: 10 in the **homicide DF**, 8 in the **agency DF**, and 6 in the **weather DF**. In the **weather DF**, `select()` with `-c()` also drops the columns I don't need, e.g., the API metadata like *timezone* and *elevation*, along with every column that starts with *daily_units*. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Rename columns to target schema. #== homicide file renames == homicide_renamed <- homicide_df %>% rename( solved_status = Solved, record_month = Month, record_year = Year, victim_age = VicAge, victim_count = VicCount, offender_age = OffAge, offender_count = OffCount, weapon_used = Weapon, relationship_status = Relationship, circumstance_status = Circumstance ) #== geojson/agency file renames == geojson_renamed <- geojson_df %>% rename( agency_name = NAME, agency_type = TYPE, agency_city = CITY, agency_state = STATE, agency_latitude = LATITUDE, agency_longitude = LONGITUDE, ft_sworn = FTSWORN, agency_population = POPULATION ) #== weather file renames + drop API metadata == weather_renamed <- weather_df %>% rename( temp_2m_avg = daily.temperature_2m_mean, relative_humidity_2m_avg = daily.relative_humidity_2m_mean, rain_sum = daily.rain_sum, snowfall_sum = daily.snowfall_sum, daily_time = daily.time, state = state_territory ) %>% # (Prabhakaran, 2026b) select( -c( generationtime_ms, utc_offset_seconds, timezone, timezone_abbreviation, elevation, location_id, starts_with("daily_units") ) ) ``` ::: My `check_column_counts()` function is run on the three renamed dataframes to confirm each one's width. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Check the renamed datasets. #== call column count function == # (Buck, 2025) check_column_counts( homicide_renamed, geojson_renamed, weather_renamed ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Homicide, Law Enforcement, and Weather columns returned. ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` $homicide_cols [1] 30 $geojson_cols [1] 37 $weather_cols [1] 8 ``` ::: ::: The **homicide DF** still has 30 columns and the **agency DF** still has 37, so renaming didn't add or drop any. The **weather DF** went from 19 columns to 8, since `select()` removed the 11 columns I didn't need. Next, I'll call `column_list()` again, this time on the renamed DFs, to confirm the new names took. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Check the new column names to confirm the renaming operation worked. #== call the column list function == # (Buck, 2025) display_columns <- column_list( data1 = homicide_renamed, data2 = geojson_renamed, data3 = weather_renamed ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` All datasets returned. ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} display_columns ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` $homicide_list [1] "ID" "CNTYFIPS" "Ori" [4] "State" "Agency" "Agentype" [7] "Source" "solved_status" "record_year" [10] "record_month" "Incident" "ActionType" [13] "Homicide" "Situation" "victim_age" [16] "VicSex" "VicRace" "VicEthnic" [19] "offender_age" "OffSex" "OffRace" [22] "OffEthnic" "weapon_used" "relationship_status" [25] "circumstance_status" "Subcircum" "victim_count" [28] "offender_count" "FileDate" "MSA" $geojson_list [1] "OBJECTID" "ID" "agency_name" [4] "ADDRESS" "agency_city" "agency_state" [7] "ZIP" "ZIP4" "TELEPHONE" [10] "agency_type" "STATUS" "agency_population" [13] "COUNTY" "COUNTYFIPS" "COUNTRY" [16] "agency_latitude" "agency_longitude" "NAICS_CODE" [19] "NAICS_DESC" "SOURCE" "SOURCEDATE" [22] "VAL_METHOD" "VAL_DATE" "WEBSITE" [25] "CI_ID" "CSLLEA08ID" "SUBTYPE1" [28] "SUBTYPE2" "TRIBAL" "NUMPRE" [31] "NUMFIXSUB" "NUMMOBILE" "ft_sworn" [34] "FTCIV" "PTSWORN" "PTCIV" [37] "geometry" $weather_list [1] "latitude" "longitude" [3] "daily_time" "temp_2m_avg" [5] "rain_sum" "snowfall_sum" [7] "relative_humidity_2m_avg" "state" ``` ::: ::: The new names show up in all three lists (for example, *solved_status*, *agency_name*, and *temp_2m_avg*). Columns I didn't rename keep their original style, such as *VicSex* in the **homicide DF** and *ADDRESS* in the **agency DF**, while the eight columns left in the **weather DF** all use lowercase words, with underscores where needed. My fourth custom function, `three_col_check()`, uses `count()` to tally the values in three columns of one DF. The `{{ }}` around each column lets me pass in plain column names, and its defaults are the victim columns *VicEthnic*, *VicRace*, and *VicSex*. Then, I'll run it on the **homicide DF** to see how victims break down by ethnicity, race, and sex, and to spot any formatting problems in the labels. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Count victim ethnicity/race/sex for category breakdown and formatting issues. #== call category column function == # (Buck, 2025) three_col_check( homicide_renamed ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` The dataframe's three columns returned. ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` $first_summary # A tibble: 3 × 2 VicEthnic n 1 Hispanic origin 97896 2 Not of Hispanic origin 294842 3 Unknown or not reported 501898 $second_summary # A tibble: 6 × 2 VicRace n 1 American Indian or Alaskan Native 7382 2 Asian 12790 3 Black 427294 4 Native Hawaiian or Pacific Islander 268 5 Unknown 11078 6 White 435824 $third_summary # A tibble: 3 × 2 VicSex n 1 Female 199567 2 Male 693403 3 Unknown 1666 ``` ::: ::: None of the three tables has an NA row, and each one adds up to 894,636 records, the full **homicide DF**. The largest *VicEthnic* group is "Unknown or not reported," with 501,898 records, more than half of the total. That label is also worded differently from *VicRace* and *VicSex*, which both use "Unknown." In *VicRace*, the two largest groups are White and Black.
::: ## Filter victims and recode victim and offender race Now, I'll narrow the **homicide DF** to female victims with a known race, using the `filter()` to keep the "Female" records in *VicSex* and drop the "Unknown" records in *VicRace*. Then, the `mutate()` with the `case_when()` to collapse the three smaller race groups, such as Asian, into one "Other Ethnic" group in *victim_race_collapsed*, and the `if_else()` turns that into a two-group *victim_racial_construct*: Black or Not Black. The result is saved as the **recoded DF**, and the `nrow()` and my custom `three_col_check()` confirm its size and categories. #### victim race recode ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Recode victim race/ethnic into binary constructs. #== victim side: filter gender, drop Unknown race, collapse categories, binary-encode == homicide_recoded <- homicide_renamed %>% filter(VicSex == "Female") %>% filter(VicRace != "Unknown") %>% mutate( # (Matt, 2020; Hadley, 2024) victim_race_collapsed = case_when( VicRace %in% c( "Asian", "American Indian or Alaskan Native", "Native Hawaiian or Pacific Islander" ) ~ "Other Ethnic", TRUE ~ VicRace # keeps "Black" and "White" as-is ), # (Hadley, 2024) victim_racial_construct = if_else( victim_race_collapsed == "Black", "Black", "Not Black" ) ) #== view recode dataset record count == nrow(homicide_recoded) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 197147 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} #== check recoded and original race constructs == # (Buck, 2025) three_col_check( data = homicide_recoded, col1 = victim_race_collapsed, col2 = victim_racial_construct, col3 = VicEthnic ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` The dataframe's three columns returned. ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` $first_summary # A tibble: 3 × 2 victim_race_collapsed n 1 Black 72849 2 Other Ethnic 6022 3 White 118276 $second_summary # A tibble: 2 × 2 victim_racial_construct n 1 Black 72849 2 Not Black 124298 $third_summary # A tibble: 3 × 2 VicEthnic n 1 Hispanic origin 14188 2 Not of Hispanic origin 68915 3 Unknown or not reported 114044 ``` ::: ::: The **recoded DF** has 197,147 records. Since the earlier victim counts showed 199,567 female victims, dropping "Unknown" race removed 2,420 more. In *victim_racial_construct*, 72,849 records are Black and 124,298 are Not Black, which is the Other Ethnic and White counts in *victim_race_collapsed* added together.
::: {.content-hidden when-profile="book"} Before recoding the offender side, I'll use `count()` to see the *OffRace* categories. This count runs on the full **homicide DF** from the renaming step, not the **recoded DF**, so it covers all 894,636 records. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Count offender race categories to confirm which values need collapsing. #== view raw OffRace category counts == homicide_renamed %>% count( OffRace ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 6 × 2 OffRace n 1 American Indian or Alaskan Native 5767 2 Asian 7819 3 Black 304272 4 Native Hawaiian or Pacific Islander 241 5 Unknown 273564 6 White 302973 ``` ::: ::: *OffRace* uses the same six labels as *VicRace*, so the same three smaller groups can be collapsed into "Other Ethnic." Unlike the victim side, "Unknown" is one of the largest offender groups, at 273,564 records. Then, `mutate()` builds the offender versions the same way, *offender_race_collapsed* and *offender_racial_construct*, but this time `case_when()` keeps "Unknown" as its own group instead of dropping it. As the code comment notes, offender race is only descriptive, so keeping these records avoids shrinking the **recoded DF**. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Recode the offender race/ethnic categories into binary constructs. #== offender side: keep Unknown as its own category (non-predictor, descriptive only) == homicide_recoded <- homicide_recoded %>% mutate( # (Matt, 2020; Hadley, 2024) offender_race_collapsed = case_when( OffRace %in% c( "Asian", "American Indian or Alaskan Native", "Native Hawaiian or Pacific Islander" ) ~ "Other Ethnic", TRUE ~ OffRace # keeps "Black", "White", "Unknown" as-is ), # (Matt, 2020; Hadley, 2024) offender_racial_construct = case_when( offender_race_collapsed == "Black" ~ "Black", offender_race_collapsed == "Unknown" ~ "Unknown", TRUE ~ "Not Black" ) ) #== check recoded race constructs == # (Buck, 2025) three_col_check( data = homicide_recoded, col1 = offender_race_collapsed, col2 = offender_racial_construct, col3 = VicEthnic ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` The dataframe's three columns returned. ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` $first_summary # A tibble: 4 × 2 offender_race_collapsed n 1 Black 62643 2 Other Ethnic 4057 3 Unknown 44871 4 White 85576 $second_summary # A tibble: 3 × 2 offender_racial_construct n 1 Black 62643 2 Not Black 89633 3 Unknown 44871 $third_summary # A tibble: 3 × 2 VicEthnic n 1 Hispanic origin 14188 2 Not of Hispanic origin 68915 3 Unknown or not reported 114044 ``` ::: ::: In *offender_racial_construct*, 62,643 records are Black, 89,633 are Not Black, and 44,871 are Unknown. The *VicEthnic* table matches the one from the victim recode exactly, so `mutate()` added the new columns without changing the number of records.
## Do feature engineering and selection Next, I'll turn to *VAL_DATE* in the **agency DF**, the date each agency's record was validated. But first, the `select()` and `head()` show five sample values, and the `class()` checks the column's data type. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Inspect the current geojson date timestamps and how they're formatted. #== view sample date values == geojson_renamed %>% select(VAL_DATE) %>% head(5) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 5 × 1 VAL_DATE 1 Tue, 14 Aug 2018 00:00:00 GMT 2 Wed, 15 Aug 2018 00:00:00 GMT 3 Tue, 12 Feb 2019 00:00:00 GMT 4 Mon, 30 Jun 2008 00:00:00 GMT 5 Wed, 06 Feb 2019 00:00:00 GMT ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} #== check date data type == class(geojson_renamed$VAL_DATE) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "character" ``` ::: ::: Each *VAL_DATE* value is written as text that starts with a short weekday name and ends with a time and "GMT" (e.g., *"Wed, 15 Aug 2018 00:00:00 GMT"*). The `class()` returns *"character"*, so the dates have to be parsed before R can read a weekday or day from them. Then, the `mutate()` with `parse_date_time()` turns *VAL_DATE* into a real date-time (*val_date_parsed*). Its `orders` argument, "a, d b Y H:M:S", describes the text's layout: weekday, day, month, year, then the time, and the `tz = "GMT"` matches the time zone written in the text. From there, the `wday()` with `label = TRUE` and `abbr = FALSE` pulls the full weekday name into *validated_week_name*, and the `day()` pulls the day of the month into *validated_day*. The result is saved as the **derived DF**, where the `sum()` with `is.na()` counts any dates that failed to parse, and the `count()` shows how the weekdays break down. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Derive validated_week_name and validated_day from VAL_DATE. #== parse for weekday fullnmae and numeric value == geojson_derived <- geojson_renamed %>% mutate( # (Spinu, 2011) val_date_parsed = parse_date_time( VAL_DATE, orders = "a, d b Y H:M:S", tz = "GMT" ), # (Spinu, 2011) validated_week_name = wday( val_date_parsed, label = TRUE, abbr = FALSE ), # (Spinu, 2011) validated_day = day(val_date_parsed) ) #== confirm no parsing failures by checking for NAs == sum( is.na( geojson_derived$val_date_parsed ) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 0 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} #== view derived weekname counts == geojson_derived %>% count(validated_week_name) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 6 × 2 validated_week_name n 1 Monday 4256 2 Tuesday 5276 3 Wednesday 5797 4 Thursday 4944 5 Friday 3212 6 Saturday 1 ``` ::: ::: The NA count is 0, so every *VAL_DATE* value parsed. The weekday counts add up to *23,486* records, the full **agency DF**. Nearly every record was validated on a weekday, with Wednesday being the most common, Sunday having no records, and only *1* record on a Saturday. To confirm the new columns line up with the original text, the `select()` and `head()` show *VAL_DATE* next to *validated_week_name* and *validated_day* for five records. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Preview derived date/day-of-week columns to confirm they were extracted. #== view sample derived date features == geojson_derived %>% select( VAL_DATE, validated_week_name, validated_day ) %>% head(5) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 5 × 3 VAL_DATE validated_week_name validated_day 1 Tue, 14 Aug 2018 00:00:00 GMT Tuesday 14 2 Wed, 15 Aug 2018 00:00:00 GMT Wednesday 15 3 Tue, 12 Feb 2019 00:00:00 GMT Tuesday 12 4 Mon, 30 Jun 2008 00:00:00 GMT Monday 30 5 Wed, 06 Feb 2019 00:00:00 GMT Wednesday 6 ``` ::: ::: In all five rows, *validated_week_name* matches the short weekday at the start of **VAL_DATE**, and *validated_day* matches its day number, for example, *Tuesday* and *14* for **"Tue, 14 Aug 2018 00:00:00 GMT."** The day number also drops the leading zero, so "06" became *6*. Now, back to the **homicide DF**. Before dropping anything, I'll look at a few candidate columns, such as *MSA* and *FileDate*. The `head()` shows samples, `sum` with `is.na` counts missing values, `count` tallies the categories, and the `summary()` describes the numbers in the *Incident* column. These checks run on the full **homicide DF** from the renaming step, and cover all **894,636 records**. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Inspect (1st five records, NAs, and value counts) candidate columns before dropping. #== MSA: metro statistical area column == homicide_renamed %>% select( MSA ) %>% head(5) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 5 × 1 MSA 1 Anchorage, AK 2 Anchorage, AK 3 Anchorage, AK 4 Anchorage, AK 5 Anchorage, AK ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} sum( is.na(homicide_renamed$MSA) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 0 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} #== file date column == homicide_renamed %>% select( FileDate ) %>% head(5) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 5 × 1 FileDate 1 30180 2 30180 3 30180 4 30180 5 30180 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} sum( is.na(homicide_renamed$FileDate) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 17075 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} #== situation column == homicide_renamed %>% count( Situation ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 6 × 2 Situation n 1 Multiple victims/multiple offenders 13721 2 Multiple victims/single offender 44596 3 Multiple victims/unknown offender(s) 19904 4 Single victim/multiple offenders 95370 5 Single victim/single offender 489422 6 Single victim/unknown offender(s) 231623 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} #== action type column == homicide_renamed %>% count( ActionType ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 2 × 2 ActionType n 1 Adjustment 150718 2 Normal update 743918 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} #== incident column == homicide_renamed %>% select( Incident ) %>% # (StatisticsDiscipline, 2021) summary() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Incident Min. : 0.00 1st Qu.: 1.00 Median : 2.00 Mean : 53.12 3rd Qu.: 11.00 Max. :27113.00 ``` ::: ::: Running the `view-unused-cols` chunk shows that the *MSA* column has no NA values, and its samples pair a city with a state abbreviation (e.g., *"Anchorage, AK"*). *FileDate* holds a number rather than a date, for example, *30180*, and has *17,075* NA values. *Situation* groups each homicide by its number of victims and offenders, with *"Single victim/single offender"* being the largest group at *489,422* records. *ActionType* has only two labels, *"Adjustment"* and *"Normal update."* And *Incident* ranges from *0.00* to *27,113.00*, with a median of *2.00*. To check whether *MSA* can be rebuilt from other columns, `mutate` with `paste0` joins the *Agency* and *State* columns with a comma and a space into *msa_reconstructed*, and the `filter()` with `nrow` counts the records where it doesn't match the *MSA* column. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Reconstruct the metropolitan area categories from the city and state columns, then count rows. #== verify MSA string alignment == homicide_renamed %>% mutate( # (Bobbitt, 2022) msa_reconstructed = paste0( Agency, ", ", State ) ) %>% filter( MSA != msa_reconstructed ) %>% nrow() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 894636 ``` ::: ::: The count is **894,636**, every record in the **homicide DF**, so the rebuilt version doesn't match *MSA* even once. Then, I'll compare just the city part. The `sub()` with the pattern `",.*"` removes the comma and everything after it from *MSA*, leaving only the city in *msa_city_only*, and the `filter()` with `nrow` counts the records where that city doesn't match *Agency*. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Extract the city name from the metropolitan area string and verify that it matches the agency name for every record. #== check agency and msa city alignment == homicide_renamed %>% mutate( # (Hemken, 2024) msa_city_only = sub( ",.*", "", MSA ) ) %>% filter( msa_city_only != Agency ) %>% nrow() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 747806 ``` ::: ::: The output shows that **747,806** records don't match, which leaves only 146,830 where the city in *MSA* is the same as *Agency*. So, for most records, *MSA* doesn't name the agency's own city. With those checks done, the `select()` with a minus sign in front of each name drops four columns from the **recoded DF**: *Subcircum*, *FileDate*, *ActionType*, and *MSA*. These columns were ruled out for the analysis, while *Situation* and *Incident* stay in. I added this column so the records with no agency population are marked as their own group instead of only showing NA. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Derive surrounding/within jurisdiction predictor. #== build the dataset == homicide_modeling_df <- homicide_final_reloaded %>% mutate( # (Matt, 2020; Hadley, 2024) jurisdiction_match = case_when( is.na(agency_population) ~ "Surrounding Area", TRUE ~ "Within Jurisdiction" ) ) #== display row count == nrow(homicide_modeling_df) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 15766 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} #== display new column == homicide_modeling_df %>% count(jurisdiction_match) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 2 × 2 jurisdiction_match n 1 Surrounding Area 2897 2 Within Jurisdiction 12869 ``` ::: ::: The **modeling DF** still has *15,766* records. Of these, *2,897* are *"Surrounding Area"* and *12,869* are *"Within Jurisdiction,"* which add up to the same total. Then, I'll check how the missing agency population overlaps with the two groups. The first `filter()` with `is.na` keeps the records with no *agency_population*, and the second uses `!is.na`, where the `!` means "not," so it keeps the records that have one. Each `count()` shows which *jurisdiction_match* groups are in them. Lastly, `count` with `group_by` and `mutate` turns the victim race counts into a percent of each jurisdiction group, saved as *group_pct*, and the `ungroup()` removes the grouping. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Check missing agency population overlapping with the jurisdiction groups. #== missing population == homicide_modeling_df %>% filter( is.na( agency_population ) ) %>% count(jurisdiction_match) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 1 × 2 jurisdiction_match n 1 Surrounding Area 2897 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} #== non-missing population == homicide_modeling_df %>% filter( !is.na( agency_population ) ) %>% count(jurisdiction_match) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 1 × 2 jurisdiction_match n 1 Within Jurisdiction 12869 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} #== display mix groups == homicide_modeling_df %>% count( jurisdiction_match, victim_racial_construct ) %>% group_by( jurisdiction_match ) %>% mutate( group_pct = n / sum(n) * 100 ) %>% ungroup() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 4 × 4 jurisdiction_match victim_racial_construct n group_pct 1 Surrounding Area Black 904 31.2 2 Surrounding Area Not Black 1993 68.8 3 Within Jurisdiction Black 4722 36.7 4 Within Jurisdiction Not Black 8147 63.3 ``` ::: ::: The missing-population check shows that all of its *2,897* records are *"Surrounding Area,"* and the non-missing check shows that all of its *12,869* records are *"Within Jurisdiction,"* so *jurisdiction_match* is just a label for whether *agency_population* is missing. In the *"Surrounding Area"* group, *31.2%* of the victims are Black, compared to *36.7%* in the *"Within Jurisdiction"* group; simply put, Black victims make up a somewhat bigger portion of the *"Within Jurisdiction"* records. ### Wrap Up ::: To finish, I'll save the **modeling DF** with `arrow::write_parquet()` as its own Parquet file in the processed data folder, separate from the **final DF**'s file.
